title: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
hook: an old send-off for graduating students says give with fear. why fear?
carry: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
tomorrow: count every can, or stop counting? one book, two answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma at a measured pace: effort sized like food and sleep, so a year of service lasts. Today, the manner of the giving.

A graduation speech can sound like a greeting card: follow your dreams, be kind, call home. An old one, in the Taittiriya Upanishad, has a teacher sending off students who've finished their study. Speak the truth, he says. Follow dharma. Honor your mother and father. Then a short list on giving, and one line in it sounds wrong. Give with fear. Not with joy, not with love. Fear. Why would a teacher send students off with that?
screen: `AN OLD GRADUATION SPEECH.` → `GIVE WITH FEAR?` → `WHY FEAR?`

segments.voice: Here's the whole list, in paraphrase. Give with faith, and don't give without it. Give from your plenty. Give with modesty. Give with fear. Give with understanding. The Sanskrit for the odd line is bhiya, with fear, and readers hear it more than one way. Some hear awe: the giver stands a little in awe of what giving is. Some hear a worry that the gift is too small, or will be given badly. Either way, look at the line beside it. Hriya, with modesty, even a little shyness. Neither word is about the size of the gift. Both are about the giver: not puffed up, not careless. The Gita takes the question further, in chapter seventeen, sorting gifts into three kinds. The clear kind is given because giving is right, to someone who can't pay it back, at a fitting place and time. The restless kind is given expecting a return, or grudgingly, with a wince. The dark kind goes to the wrong place, at the wrong time, without respect, even with contempt. All three are gifts; something changes hands every time. But a gift carries more than the thing. Contempt rides along. So does a hidden invoice. So does respect. That's the puzzle, close to solved: the fear is the opposite of swagger. And it's the third design rule for a year of service. Plan the manner, not just the amount.
screen: `GIVE WITH FAITH, MODESTY, FEAR.` · `BHIYA: AWE, OR WORRY IT'S TOO SMALL.` · `THE GITA'S THREE KINDS OF GIFT.` · then, large: `PLAN THE MANNER, NOT JUST THE AMOUNT.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms open and turned up, the way someone holds out a gift. Keep them there through the sit. Bring to mind one gift you could give with nobody watching, and let your open hands hold it quietly.
Karma, in the giving: with faith, with modesty, with a little awe, so the gift carries respect and no invoice.
For the road: karma, a year designed and reviewed, and given with modesty. See you tomorrow.

notes: Karma service capstone, day 4 of 7 (1651–1657): the manner of giving. 'The third design rule' follows 1651 and 1653.

Taittiriya 1.11.3: shraddhaya deyam, ashraddhaya adeyam, shriya deyam, hriya deyam, bhiya deyam, samvida deyam. Rendered faith / not without faith / from plenty / modesty / fear / understanding; 'shriya' and 'samvida' have other readings (with grace; with friendliness). Confirm.

The two readings of bhiya (awe; worry that the gift is too small or given badly) are offered as readings ('some hear'); confirm both are fair to the commentaries (Shankara reads it as fear, i.e. with awe/apprehension).

Gita 17.20–22 paraphrased (the clear gift to one who cannot return it, at the right place and time, to a worthy person; the restless gift with expectation of return or reluctantly; the dark gift at the wrong place and time, to unworthy persons, without respect, with contempt). Confirm.
